Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Former New York City police Commissioner Bernard Kerik pleaded not guilty in federal court Monday to a revised indictment charging him in a corruption and tax evasion case, according to a spokesman for the New York District Attorney. A revised indictment brings to 15 the number of counts against former police Commissioner Bernard Kerik. The revised indictment includes two new counts of aiding the filing of false returns and a charge involving making false statements while applying for a housing loan, spokesman Herbert Hadad of the district attorney's office told CNN. Kerik is accused of failing to report more than $500,000 in income between 1999 and 2004, said Patricia Haynes, the IRS agent in charge of the case. Prosecutors allege Kerik received and concealed benefits of about $255,000 in renovations to his Riverdale, New York, apartment from a company seeking to do business with the city of New York. Revisions to the original indictment, which included charges of corruption, conspiracy and tax evasion, bring to 15 the number of counts against Kerik. Barry Berke, Kerik's attorney, declined to comment. The indictment also charges that Kerik made several false statements to the White House and other federal officials when he applied for the position as adviser to the Homeland Security Advisory Council, to the Coalition Provisional Authority in Iraq and in connection with his nomination to be secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. U.S. District Judge Stephen Robinson did not rule Monday on whether the two counts that include charges of lying to White House officials will be tried in Washington or White Plains, New York. Kerik is due back in court February 3 for a hearing on pretrial motions, Hadad said. A trial date has not been set. Kerik, 53, is a longtime friend and former protege of former Mayor Rudy Giuliani. President Bush nominated him to be secretary of homeland security after winning re-election in 2004, but Kerik withdrew his name amid allegations that he employed a nanny who had a questionable immigration status. Bronx District Attorney Robert Johnson began investigating allegations that Kerik had traded payment on repairs to his Bronx apartment for favors, including city contracts. The former chief pleaded guilty in 2006 to accepting tens of thousands of dollars in gifts while he worked as city corrections commissioner. He was fined $221,000 and avoided jail time under his plea agreement. Before tapping Kerik for a Cabinet post, Bush dispatched him to Baghdad to train Iraqi police after the U.S. invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein. He left three months into an expected six-month stint, with Iraqi officials telling reporters that he had completed his assignment. In 2004, he campaigned for Bush's re-election and spoke at the Republican National Convention in New York. CNN's Mary Snow contributed to this report.

The updated indictment raises the total number of charges against Kerik to 15. Hadad said the new allegations include two counts of assisting in the submission of fraudulent tax returns and one count related to false information allegedly provided on a housing-loan application.

Patricia Haynes, the IRS agent overseeing the investigation, said Kerik is accused of not declaring more than $500,000 in income from 1999 through 2004. Prosecutors also claim he accepted and hid approximately $255,000 worth of renovations to his apartment in Riverdale, New York, from a company that wanted to conduct business with New York City.

The original indictment already contained corruption, conspiracy and tax-evasion charges. Kerik’s lawyer, Barry Berke, declined to discuss the case.

Kerik is also accused of making multiple false statements to White House personnel and other federal officials while seeking several government roles. Those positions included adviser to the Homeland Security Advisory Council, service with the Coalition Provisional Authority in Iraq and secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

U.S. District Judge Stephen Robinson did not decide Monday whether two counts involving alleged lies to White House officials should be prosecuted in Washington or in White Plains, New York. Hadad said Kerik is scheduled to return to court on February 3 for a hearing on pretrial motions. No trial date has been established.

Kerik, 53, has long been a friend and former protégé of ex-New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani. After his 2004 re-election, President Bush selected Kerik to lead the Department of Homeland Security. Kerik later withdrew from consideration after claims surfaced that he had hired a nanny whose immigration status was in question.

Bronx District Attorney Robert Johnson opened an investigation into accusations that Kerik exchanged favors—including city contracts—for payment of repair work at his Bronx apartment.

In 2006, the former police chief admitted guilt to accepting gifts valued at tens of thousands of dollars during his tenure as the city’s corrections commissioner. Under the plea arrangement, he paid a $221,000 fine and received no prison sentence.

Before nominating Kerik for the Cabinet, Bush sent him to Baghdad following the U.S. invasion that removed Saddam Hussein from power. His task was to train Iraqi police officers. Although the assignment was expected to last six months, Kerik departed after three months; Iraqi officials told journalists that his work had been completed.

Kerik also supported Bush’s 2004 re-election campaign and delivered remarks at that year’s Republican National Convention in New York.

# Kerik pleads not guilty to revised federal corruption indictment

**WHITE PLAINS, New York (CNN)** — Former New York City Police Commissioner Bernard Kerik pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a revised federal indictment charging him with 15 counts involving corruption, tax evasion and false statements.

The superseding indictment accuses Kerik of accepting valuable renovations to his Bronx apartment from a construction company seeking city business and failing to report the benefit as income. Prosecutors also allege he concealed information from federal officials and made false statements during the vetting process for a Cabinet position.

Kerik entered his plea in federal court in White Plains. He has denied wrongdoing through his attorneys.

The charges include conspiracy, tax-related offenses and lying to government officials. Prosecutors allege the renovations were worth hundreds of thousands of dollars and were provided while Kerik held influential New York City posts.

Kerik served as police commissioner under then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani and became a prominent public figure after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. President George W. Bush nominated him to lead the Department of Homeland Security in 2004, but Kerik withdrew amid questions about his personal and financial affairs.

The revised indictment replaces an earlier version of the federal case but continues to center on allegations that Kerik failed to disclose income and financial relationships and misled investigators.

Kerik previously pleaded guilty to state misdemeanor charges related to accepting the apartment renovations while he was a city official. The federal case carries the possibility of a substantial prison sentence if he is convicted.

### Status and “new” federal charges

The federal prosecution of former New York City Police Commissioner Bernard Kerik is no longer pending. The major expansion of the case occurred in 2008, when prosecutors filed a superseding indictment adding or revising allegations that Kerik lied to White House officials during the 2004 vetting process for his nomination as secretary of homeland security.

The broader federal case accused Kerik of:

- Accepting roughly **$250,000 in apartment renovations** from people connected to Interstate Industrial Corp., a contractor seeking New York City business, while Kerik was corrections commissioner.
- Using his public position to assist the company despite concerns about its alleged organized-crime connections.
- Failing to report the renovations and other income on tax returns and government disclosure forms.
- Making false statements on loan applications and to federal officials.
- Concealing relevant financial relationships from White House personnel considering him for the homeland-security post.

Kerik initially pleaded not guilty. In **November 2009**, however, he pleaded guilty to **eight felony counts**, including tax offenses and making false statements. In **February 2010**, he was sentenced to four years in federal prison. He was released in 2013, and President Donald Trump granted him a **full pardon in February 2020**.

### Political background

Kerik rose from undercover narcotics work and the New York Police Department to become Mayor **Rudolph Giuliani’s corrections commissioner** and then NYPD commissioner from 2000 through 2001. His public profile increased sharply after the September 11 attacks, and he became a close Giuliani political ally.

President George W. Bush nominated Kerik to lead the Department of Homeland Security in December 2004. Kerik withdrew within days, initially citing his failure to pay taxes for a household employee. Subsequent scrutiny of his finances, business relationships and disclosures helped lead to the state and federal investigations.

In later years Kerik remained active in Republican politics, supported Trump, and assisted efforts challenging the 2020 presidential-election results. The 2020 pardon removed the federal consequences of his conviction, but it did not erase the historical record of the charges or guilty plea.

## Bernard Kerik case: Apartment renovations, concealed income and false statements led to prison sentence

**NEW YORK —** Bernard Kerik, the former New York City police commissioner once nominated to lead the Department of Homeland Security, faced a wide-ranging federal corruption and tax prosecution centered on allegations that he concealed valuable apartment renovations, failed to report taxable income and gave false information to government officials.

The case is no longer pending. Kerik pleaded guilty in November 2009, was sentenced in February 2010 and later received a presidential pardon from Donald Trump in February 2020. Consequently, there are no upcoming proceedings in the original criminal prosecution.

### Renovations supplied by a city contractor

At the heart of the case were approximately **$255,000 in renovations** to Kerik’s apartment in the Riverdale section of the Bronx. Prosecutors said the work was paid for by Interstate Industrial Corp., a construction company that was seeking city business while Kerik held senior positions in Mayor Rudolph Giuliani’s administration.

Federal authorities alleged that Kerik accepted the renovations while serving as New York City correction commissioner and then took steps to hide who had paid for them. The government characterized the work as a benefit that should have been disclosed both as part of Kerik’s public responsibilities and on his tax returns.

Interstate Industrial had sought approval to work on city projects but faced scrutiny over alleged organized-crime associations. The company disputed suggestions that it was controlled by organized crime. Prosecutors nevertheless argued that Kerik’s failure to disclose the financial relationship was particularly serious because the contractor had business before the city.

### Allegedly unreported income

The federal indictment accused Kerik of failing to report the renovations and other income to the Internal Revenue Service. Contemporary accounts of the prosecution described the total omitted taxable income as **more than $500,000 over several tax years**, with the apartment work representing a major portion of that amount.

The tax case covered returns for 1999 through 2001. Prosecutors said Kerik obstructed the IRS and filed false returns by excluding benefits and payments that should have been treated as income.

Kerik ultimately admitted tax offenses as part of his guilty plea. The plea avoided a trial on the broader indictment, which initially contained 16 felony counts, including tax, fraud, obstruction and false-statement allegations.

### False statements during federal vetting

The prosecution also grew out of Kerik’s nomination in December 2004 to become secretary of homeland security. President George W. Bush selected him for the post, but Kerik withdrew days later, initially citing immigration and tax problems involving a household employee.

Investigators subsequently examined statements Kerik had made during federal background checks and interviews. Prosecutors said he falsely denied or concealed his financial relationship with the contractor responsible for the apartment renovations. He was also accused of making misleading statements to White House personnel and other federal officials reviewing his suitability for a Cabinet-level position.

The government alleged that Kerik falsely represented that he had no disqualifying financial dealings with people seeking to do business with New York City. Similar concealment allegations arose from disclosures he made to city authorities.

### Guilty plea and sentence

On **Nov. 5, 2009**, Kerik pleaded guilty in federal court in White Plains, New York, to **eight felony counts**, including tax charges and making false statements. In court, he acknowledged that he had failed to report income and had provided false information to federal officials.

On **Feb. 18, 2010**, U.S. District Judge Stephen C. Robinson sentenced Kerik to **four years in federal prison**, a term longer than the sentence contemplated in his plea agreement. The judge said Kerik’s conduct was especially troubling because of the senior law-enforcement positions he had held and the public trust placed in him.

Kerik began serving the sentence in 2010 and was released from federal custody in 2013, completing the remainder under community supervision.

### Pardon closed the federal case

On **Feb. 18, 2020**, President Trump granted Kerik a full pardon. The pardon forgave the federal convictions but did not erase the historical record of the guilty plea or the underlying conduct Kerik admitted in court.

Thus, references in older reports to “upcoming court proceedings” generally concern either Kerik’s 2009 plea proceedings or his February 2010 sentencing. **No further trial, sentencing or appeal is currently scheduled in the original corruption and tax-evasion case.**

# Former NYPD commissioner Bernard Kerik pleads not guilty to federal corruption charges

**The onetime Homeland Security nominee and close associate of Rudy Giuliani faced allegations of fraud, tax offenses and making false statements**

**NEW YORK —** Bernard Kerik, the former New York City police commissioner whose rise to national prominence was closely tied to former Mayor Rudy Giuliani, pleaded not guilty to a wide-ranging federal indictment accusing him of corruption, tax fraud and lying to government officials.

Kerik entered the plea in November 2007 after prosecutors charged him with 16 felony counts. The indictment alleged that he accepted roughly $250,000 in renovations to his Bronx apartment from a construction company seeking city business and then concealed the benefit from authorities. Prosecutors also accused him of failing to report income and of providing false information during federal background checks.

Kerik denied wrongdoing at the time and was released on bond. His attorneys portrayed the case as an overreach arising from matters that had already been scrutinized by state authorities.

The federal prosecution marked a dramatic reversal for a law-enforcement official who had become one of the most recognizable members of Giuliani’s administration, particularly after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

## Earlier conviction over apartment renovations

Before the federal indictment, Kerik had already pleaded guilty in 2006 to two misdemeanor charges in New York. The case centered on renovations to his apartment that were paid for by a company seeking to do business with the city.

Kerik acknowledged that he failed to properly disclose the benefit and that he had improperly accepted it while serving as a city official. He avoided jail but paid fines.

The company involved had been linked by authorities to organized-crime figures, although Kerik said he did not know about those alleged connections when the work was performed.

The federal case went substantially further than the earlier state proceeding. In 2009, Kerik ultimately pleaded guilty to eight felony counts, including tax fraud and making false statements. A federal judge sentenced him in 2010 to four years in prison.

President Donald Trump granted Kerik a full pardon in 2020.

## Homeland Security nomination withdrawn

Kerik’s legal and financial problems first drew broad national attention in December 2004, shortly after President George W. Bush nominated him to lead the Department of Homeland Security.

The selection was backed by Giuliani, who praised Kerik’s leadership and experience. But Kerik withdrew his name within days, saying he had employed an undocumented immigrant as a nanny and had failed to pay the required taxes.

Additional questions soon emerged about his finances, business dealings and disclosures. The collapse of the nomination transformed what had been expected to be the next stage of Kerik’s public career into the beginning of years of legal scrutiny.

## Role in postwar Iraq

Kerik had also worked in Iraq following the 2003 US-led invasion. The Bush administration sent him to Baghdad to help rebuild and organize the Iraqi Interior Ministry and police forces.

His tenure was brief. Kerik served as a senior security adviser during a chaotic period marked by looting, insurgent violence and the breakdown of Iraqi institutions.

Supporters cited the assignment as evidence of his reputation as a forceful crisis manager. Critics later questioned both the effectiveness of the reconstruction effort and the decision to place Kerik in such a prominent role.

## A career intertwined with Giuliani

Kerik’s ascent was inseparable from his relationship with Giuliani.

After serving as a New York City police officer and corrections official, Kerik was appointed correction commissioner by Giuliani and later became NYPD commissioner in 2000. He led the department during the September 11 attacks and their aftermath, appearing frequently alongside the mayor.

Kerik later joined Giuliani Partners, the former mayor’s consulting firm. Giuliani strongly supported Kerik’s Homeland Security nomination and initially defended his former commissioner as controversies mounted.

Their relationship was tested by Kerik’s legal problems, which also created political complications for Giuliani during his 2008 presidential campaign. Giuliani said he had made a mistake by recommending Kerik for the federal post and acknowledged that the vetting had been insufficient.

Despite those strains, the two men remained publicly connected over the years. Kerik later became an outspoken ally of Giuliani and Trump.

Kerik’s trajectory — from police commissioner and prospective Cabinet secretary to convicted felon and later presidential pardon recipient — became one of the most striking falls from power among the public officials who rose to national prominence after September 11.
